title: What does my opponent want

card.idea: Section 3 taught you to scan for his checks and captures. That question is about next move, and on a quiet board it comes back empty. This one is different: what is he trying to do over the next three or four moves? Find the square his plan needs, then get there first. A plan you take away is cheaper than one you have to answer.
card.habit: Ask what square his plan needs, then stand on it.

explain.text: Run the old scan and it returns nothing: Black has no check and no capture anywhere. That does not mean he has no plan. The rook on b8 and the pawns on a6 and b7 are three men pointing at one move, b5, and b5 hits c4. The scan misses it because it is not due next move.

a4 is the answer, and it is not a threat. Before it, one white pawn covered b5. After it, two do, a4 and c4, and the pawn he has spent three men preparing now runs into both of them. Nothing has been attacked and nothing has been won. His plan has simply stopped being available.

Same shell, different intention. No a6 pawn here and the rook is on e8, so b5 is not what he is building. The pawn on d6 and the knight on d7 both cover e5, and e5 hits d4. Same empty scan, same three-man preparation, different square. Read the men, not the move list.

challenges.prompt: Run the scan you learned in Section 3 first: every black check, every black capture. What does it come back with?
options: One check and one capture; he is threatening to take on e4.
Nothing at all. Black has no check and no capture anywhere on this board.
Two captures, both on the queenside.

hints.text: Go through his men one at a time. Which of them touches a white man?

challenges.reason: Not one black man attacks a white man, and nothing of his reaches the white king. There is no pawn on e4 to take, either. The scan is not broken; it is answering a different question from the one this lesson asks.

challenges.prompt: No check and no capture. So what is Black actually preparing?
options: b5. The pawn on a6 already backs it up, the rook on b8 is behind it, and b5 hits the pawn on c4.
Nothing. A man with no check and no capture has no plan.

hints.text: Three black men are lined up on one file and one of them is a pawn that has not moved.

challenges.reason: b5 is legal right now and it is the move all three of those men are for. Nxe4 is not even legal: e4 is an empty square, because White's pawn is on e3.

challenges.prompt: Name the square before you defend it. Tap the square Black's b-pawn is heading for.

hints.text: It is two squares in front of the pawn, and it touches one of your pawns.

challenges.reason: b5 attacks c4. That single square is his whole plan, which is what makes it something you can take away rather than something you have to answer.

challenges.prompt: Right now one white pawn covers that square. Tap the square a white pawn goes to so that two of them do.

hints.text: Only one white pawn move changes the count at all.

challenges.reason: Only c4 covers b5 at the moment. a4 is the one pawn move in the position that makes it two, and it neither attacks anything nor asks Black a question.

challenges.prompt: White plays a4 to take the square away. Is the pawn safe there?
reasons: No. The pawn on a6 takes it.
No. The knight on d7 gets to c5 and hits it.
Yes. Nothing of Black's touches a4, and the rook on a1 stands behind it anyway.

hints.text: A black pawn on a6 attacks b5, not a4.

challenges.reason: No black man attacks a4. The pawn on a6 captures forwards on to b5, and c5 is covered by White's own pawn on d4, so the knight cannot go there either.

challenges.prompt: This is the board after a4. Tap every white pawn that now attacks b5.

hints.text: Two of them, one on each side of the square.

challenges.reason: a4 and c4. His break is still legal and now it simply loses a pawn, which is the whole difference a quiet move can make.

challenges.prompt: Same white setup, different black one. He again has no check and no capture. What is he preparing here?
options: Nothing is happening: the position is locked and neither side has a move that matters.
b5, which the pawn on a6 supports.
e5. The pawn on d6 and the knight on d7 both cover e5 already, and e5 hits the pawn on d4.

hints.text: Look for the square two black men already cover that also touches a white pawn.

challenges.reason: There is no pawn on a6 on this board, so nothing supports b5. e5 is legal, d6 and d7 both cover it, and it hits d4. Same empty scan as before, different square.

challenges.prompt: Tap every black man that already covers the square his pawn is heading for.

hints.text: One is a pawn and one is a knight. The knight on f6 is not one of them.

challenges.reason: The pawn on d6 and the knight on d7 cover e5. The knight on f6 looks as though it should, and it does not: from f6 it covers d5, d7, e4, g4, h5 and e8.

challenges.prompt: Play his plan for him so you know what you are stopping. Black breaks, White takes, Black takes back.
challenges.reason: After e5 dxe5 dxe5 Black has a pawn on e5, the d-file is open for the queen on d8 and the knight on d7 has c5 and e5 to think about. Playing his idea out is how you find out whether it is worth stopping.

takeaway: His checks and captures answer what he can do next move. Ask instead what square his next three moves need, and take it before he gets there.
